Spawning in Bigeye ilisha (Ilisha megaloptera) typically occurs in coastal waters during the warmer months, with environmental temperature playing a critical role in reproductive physiology. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 9% [GSI = 9%] at a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This species produces small, pelagic eggs with a diameter of approximately 1.46 mm, from which the dry weight at birth can be estimated. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae have a calculated dry weight of 0.0016 grams [Wwb = 0.0016 grams], a value consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by the small egg size typical of clupeiform fishes. The onset of exogenous feeding follows shortly after yolk absorption, and the age at birth at the same temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a developmental pace comparable to that observed in the European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus.

As larvae progress through the pelagic planktonic phase, they undergo a series of morphological transformations culminating in juvenile recruitment. The standard length at which individuals typically reach puberty has been determined to be 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the ability to participate in spawning aggregations. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 12.7 grams [Wwp = 12.7 grams] was derived from length-weight relationships established for local populations, providing a useful metric for assessing the condition of sub-adult fish entering the reproductive stock. Individuals that successfully attain this size threshold divert increasing energetic resources toward gametogenesis, a shift reflected in the seasonal elevation of the gonadosomatic index. The transition from juvenile to mature stages is thus tightly linked to both somatic growth and the prevailing thermal regime, which modulates metabolic rates and food availability.

The ultimate standard length recorded for Bigeye ilisha approaches 36.5 centimeters [Li = 36.5 centimeters], representing the maximum size achieved by the oldest and fastest-growing individuals in the population. This asymptotic size corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 587 grams [Wwi = 587 grams], a substantial body mass that positions Ilisha megaloptera among the larger members of the Pristigasteridae family. Field surveys suggest that growth to this maximum dimension requires several years of consistent feeding in productive estuarine and nearshore habitats. The length-weight relationship employed to estimate ultimate mass follows a power function typical of fusiform fish, where the exponent approaches three, indicating isometric scaling of body width and depth relative to length. Attaining this size confers reproductive advantages, as larger females are capable of producing more numerous clutches of eggs.

In terms of overall longevity, the maximum lifespan for Bigeye ilisha has been estimated at 730 days [am = 730 days] under the reference temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, approximately two years [am = approximately two years], is characteristic of many small-to-medium-sized clupeiform species that exhibit rapid early growth and early reproductive maturity at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Survival to the oldest age classes is influenced by predation pressure and fishing mortality, both of which can truncate the age distribution in heavily exploited stocks. The life cycle is thus compressed into a brief window of somatic growth followed by intensive reproductive effort, a strategy that maximizes population turnover in variable coastal environments. Individuals that avoid capture and natural predators may spawn over multiple seasons, though the energetic demands of repeated spawning likely curtail survival beyond the second year.

Reproductive output during each spawning event has been documented in several studies of Bigeye ilisha, providing valuable parameters for stock assessment. Females produce an average of 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch], and the reproductive schedule involves approximately 3 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 3 clutches annually] during the spawning season. When these two components are combined, the annual egg production per female is moderate, reflecting the species' relatively small body size and abbreviated lifespan. Population models incorporating these life-history traits indicate that Bigeye ilisha maintains stable recruitment under moderate fishing pressure, though the species remains sensitive to environmental fluctuations that affect early larval survival and food availability in coastal nursery grounds.
